terminal_bridge:
::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From Multi-Agent Coordination to Distributed Observability"}
Coordinating distributed agentic execution across dynamic DAG topologies and isolated sandboxes shifts the engineering bottleneck from execution to diagnosis. When an autonomous pipeline spanning multiple workers, worktrees, and tool invocations stalls or produces an erroneous integration after hundreds of thousands of tokens, passive inspection of raw chat transcripts is utterly insufficient for determining fault etiology. Was the failure triggered by an ambiguous parent task envelope, an unhandled merge conflict in an optimistic worktree reconciliation, a latent correlation in worker model weights, or a silent lease expiration in the capability gateway?

Operating distributed agent fleets and stateful single-agent runtimes in production demands comprehensive, fine-grained telemetry that exposes causal execution trajectories. In Chapter 16 (*System Observability*), we develop the telemetry infrastructure required to monitor, trace, and evaluate non-deterministic systems: structured OpenTelemetry spans adapted for autoregressive decode loops, interactive evaluation environments and gyms, statistical confidence bounds on non-deterministic trajectory success, and post-mortem causal attribution for multi-agent cascades.
:::
cumulative_ledger: Section 15.1 (The Delegation Trade-Off): Multi-agent delegation is justified only when domain specialization or parallel exploration outweighs the significant overhead of duplicated context, inter-agent serialization, and integration reconciliation.

Section 15.2 (Coordination Topologies): Multi-agent coordination requires formal task dependency graphs (DAGs) choosing between Supervisor-Worker, Linear Pipeline, and Decentralized Peer topologies based on data flow dependencies.

Section 15.3 (Typed Task Envelopes): Handoffs between agents must carry explicit, typed task envelopes (task identity, input artifact versions, delegated authority, compute budget, and completion status) rather than unstructured natural language chat.

Section 15.4 (Optimistic Concurrency Control): Concurrent agent execution against shared environments requires optimistic concurrency control, isolated branch workspaces, and three-way reconciliation to handle conflicting mutations.

Section 15.5 (Correlated Ensemble Failures): Multi-agent consensus (majority voting, peer review) does not prove semantic correctness; when agents share the same base model or training data, their failure modes are strongly correlated.

Section 15.6 (Cancellation Cascades): When an agent in a coordination graph fails or is cancelled, the runtime must propagate cancellation signals across the dependency tree and enforce backpressure to prevent worker starvation.

Section 15.7 (Attenuated Capability Delegation): Child agents must operate under strictly attenuated capability tokens derived from the parent, ensuring no delegated agent possesses more authority than its invoker.

Section 15.8 (Single-Agent Baseline Benchmarking): Any multi-agent architecture must be empirically benchmarked against an optimized single-agent baseline on identical task distributions, measuring quality, critical-path makespan, and total token expenditure.
